extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, and typesetters using The Chicago Manual of Style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for punctuation, dashes, parentheses/brackets, slashes, quotation marks, apostrophes, spacing, multiple punctuation, list and outline formatting, and recommended dictionaries/spelling practices per The Chicago Manual of Style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes and quotation marks when a break belongs to surrounding sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the break belongs to the surrounding sentence rather than to the quoted material, the em dashes must appear outside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “Someday he’s going to hit one of those long shots, and”—his voice turned huffy—“I won’t be there to see it.” (Shows placement of em dash outside closing quote when interruption belongs to surrounding sentence.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash before expressions such as “that is” or “namely”
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash may be used before expressions such as that is or namely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related examples 6.51 and 6.58 (used to introduce an explanatory or parenthetic expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A question mark or an exclamation point—but never a comma, a colon, or a semicolon—may precede an em dash; a period may precede an em dash if it is part of an abbreviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Without further warning—but what could we have done to dissuade her?—she left the plant. Only if—heaven forbid!—you lose your passport should you call home. (Comma/colon/semicolon should not precede an em dash.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash in place of comma between dependent and independent clause
rubrics_metrics.description: If the context calls for an em dash where a comma would ordinarily separate a dependent clause from an independent clause, the comma is omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Because the data had not been fully analyzed—let alone collated—the publication of the report was delayed. (Omit the comma when em dash used.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash indicating interruption in quoted material (omit comma before speaker ID)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an em dash is used at the end of quoted material to indicate an interruption, the comma can be safely omitted before the words that identify the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “T assure you, we shall never—” Sylvia began, but Mark cut her short. (No comma required before speaker tag when em dash indicates interruption.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes and line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: In printed publications, line breaks should generally be made after an em dash but not before; do not break a closing quotation mark and dash at the end of a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reflowable electronic formats, let the software determine such breaks. See also cross-references 6.87, 6.89, 7.36-47.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes used instead of quotation marks for dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Em dashes are occasionally used instead of quotation marks to set off dialogue (as in some European languages): each speech starts a new paragraph; no space follows the dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example lines: —Will he obtain the necessary signatures? —Of course he will! (Each speech begins with an em dash and a new paragraph.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dashes in lists, indexes, and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Em dashes are sometimes used like bullet points in vertical lists (informal), may be used for subentries in an index, and in tables can indicate an otherwise blank/empty cell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage as bullets is best avoided in formal prose; in tables an em dash may stand for missing data (see 3.67 and 16.27).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2-em dash for missing words or parts of words
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2-em dash represents a missing word or part of a word, omitted to disguise a name or missing/illegible in quoted/reprinted material; spacing depends on whether whole word or part is missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a whole word is missing, space appears on both sides of the dash; when only part is missing, no space appears between dash and existing letters. Examples: “The region gives its —to the language spoken there.” Admiral N— and Lady R—. Do not confuse with an underscore blank (use __ for fill-in blanks).

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-em dash in bibliographies for repeated author
rubrics_metrics.description: In a bibliography, a 3-em dash followed by a period represents the same author(s) or editor(s) named in the preceding entry; best applied by publisher or manuscript editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it can obscure information, authors normally should not supply it; example: Chaudhuri, Amit. Odysseus Abroad. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 2015. ——..A Strange and Sublime Address. London: Minerva, 1992.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parentheses to set off material
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses—stronger than a comma and similar to the dash—are used to set off material from the surrounding text and can enclose text that has no grammatical relationship to the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: He suspected that the noble gases (helium, neon, etc.) could produce a similar effect. Use parentheses for references, glosses, translations, and other as cross-referenced (see 6.129, 13.64-72, chapter 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for glosses or translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses are used to enclose glosses of unfamiliar terms or translations from other languages—or if the term is given in English, to enclose the original word; in quoted matter, use brackets instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dichtung und Wahrheit (also known as Wahrheit und Dichtung) has been translated as Poetry and Truth. For quoted matter, use [brackets] (see 6.99).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses within parentheses (use brackets inside)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some publications permit parentheses within parentheses, Chicago prefers using brackets within parentheses (especially for bibliographic purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: British style often prefers parentheses within parentheses; for mathematics see chapter 12 (12.26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: An opening parenthesis should be preceded by a comma or semicolon only in an enumeration; a closing parenthesis should never be preceded by a comma, semicolon, or colon. Question marks, exclamation points, and closing quotation marks precede a closing parenthesis if they belong to the parenthetical matter; they follow it if they belong to the surrounding sentence. A period precedes the closing parenthesis if the entire sentence is in parentheses; otherwise it follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid enclosing more than one sentence within another sentence. Parentheses may appear back to back with a space if they enclose unrelated material; sometimes use a single set separated by semicolon instead. See table 6.1 and chapter cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of square brackets for editorial interpolations and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Square brackets enclose material usually added by someone other than the original writer—editorial interpolations, explanations, translations, or corrections; sometimes bracketed material replaces rather than amplifies the original word(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “They [the free-silver Democrats] asserted that the ratio could be maintained.” Use brackets for editorial notes, corrections, and clarifications in quoted/reprinted material (see 13.59-63).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate when quoted matter already includes brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: If quoted matter already includes brackets of its own, the editor should state this in the source citation (e.g., “brackets in the original”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps readers know whether bracketed material is editorial or original; see 13.62 for italics-analogous situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square brackets in translated text (original-language terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: In translated works, square brackets are sometimes used to enclose a word or phrase in the original language; translators should use this sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The differences between society [Gesellschaft] and community [Gemeinschaft] will now be analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square brackets as parentheses within parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago prefers square brackets as parentheses within parentheses, usually for bibliographic purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (For further discussion see Richardson’s excellent analysis [1999] and Danneberger’s survey [2000].) For mathematical groupings, see chapter 12 (12.26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Square brackets in phonetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Square brackets may be used to enclose a phonetic transcription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The verb entretenir [Atratnir], like keep, is used in many idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square brackets with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the same punctuation principles apply to brackets as to parentheses; bracketed material is usually treated as if it were parenthetical, though the appearance and positioning of punctuation may depend on the source being quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrasts show proper placement of commas and brackets in quoted transcriptions; treat bracketed interpolations as parenthetical unless context dictates otherwise (see 14.145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle brackets and braces usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Angle brackets (<...>) denote mathematical delimiters or are used to enclose tags in XML and related markup; braces ({}) are used in programming and mathematical writing and are not interchangeable with parentheses or brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago discourages using angle brackets to enclose URLs in regular prose; angle brackets may be used to enclose typesetting instructions in manuscripts (see 2.81); braces appear in specialized contexts (see 12.28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other names for the slash and its general roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The slash (/) is also known as virgule, solidus, slant, or forward slash; it has several distinct uses including indicating alternatives, abbreviations, fractions, and paths/URLs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Richard Eckersley et al., Glossary of Typesetting Terms for niceties of terminology (bibliog. 2.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slash to signify alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A slash most commonly signifies alternatives as a shorthand for or; when open compounds are separated by slashes, include spaces for legibility; occasionally it can include a sense of and, but often a hyphen is better for and.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: he/she, Hercules/Heracles, his/her. For open compounds use space before and after slash. Use with care in formal prose; see 6.107.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slash for two-year spans
rubrics_metrics.description: A slash is sometimes used in dates instead of an en dash to indicate the last part of one year and the first part of the next (e.g., 1966/67).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The winter of 1966/67 was especially severe. Combine with en dash as needed for ranges (see 6.78 and 9.64).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slashes with dates (avoid all-numeral dates; use ISO if necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slashes (or periods or hyphens) are used informally in all-numeral dates (e.g., 3/10/02) but should be avoided in formal writing and where clarity is essential; if all-numeral format must be used, use ISO format YYYY-MM-DD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note regional ambiguity: U.S. month/day vs day/month elsewhere. See 9.36 for ISO recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slashes in abbreviations and as fraction bars
rubrics_metrics.description: A slash may stand for per (e.g., 110 km/sec, $450/week) or be used in certain abbreviations (c/o, n/a); it can also denote fractions when a fraction bar is impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, prefer single-glyph fractions rather than numeric slashes (e.g., use ½ instead of 1/2); see 12.45 for fraction guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slashes to show line breaks in quoted poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more lines of poetry are quoted in regular text, slashes with a space on each side are used to indicate line breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “Thou hast not missed one thought that could be fit, / And all that was improper dost omit.” See 13.29.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slashes in URLs and other paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Slashes separate directories and file names in URLs and paths; spaces are never used in such contexts. In typeset paths, a line break may occur before a slash but not between two slashes. Some systems use backslashes or colons instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: http://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/help.html. See 7.46 and 14.17 for line-break behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slashes and line breaks in printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In printed publications where slashes signal alternatives, a line break should be made after the slash, never before; avoid carrying a single character to the next line; fractions should not be broken at line end. For URLs, a line break should be made before the slash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reflowable electronic formats let software decide such breaks. See 7.46 for URL break rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks relative to other punctuation and text
rubrics_metrics.description: Location of closing quotation marks relative to punctuation follows specific rules (see cross-references 6.9–11); see specific rules for commas, colons, question marks, exclamation points with quotation marks and titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dialogue and quoted matter see chapter 13; for use with single words/phrases see 7.57, 7.60, 7.63; for foreign-language quotation marks see chapter 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of “smart” (directional) quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Published works should use directional (“smart” or curly) quotation marks that match the surrounding typeface rather than the unidirectional straight quote used by typewriters and some software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure left and right quotation marks are the proper characters; Unicode code points: left double U+201C, right double U+201D, left single U+2018, right single/apostrophe U+2019. Avoid using the straight ASCII quote (").

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the apostrophe (three main uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apostrophe’s three main uses are to indicate the possessive case, to stand in for missing letters or numerals (contractions), and—in rare instances—to form the plural of certain expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For possessive details see 7.16–7.29 and 5.20; for contractions see 7.30; for plurals of expressions see 7.5–15 (especially 7.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of “smart” apostrophes and common pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Published works should use directional (smart) apostrophes (Unicode U+2019). Two common pitfalls are using the default unidirectional mark (') and using the left single quotation mark (‘) instead of the apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software may automatically convert apostrophes incorrectly; authors and editors must override automation when necessary and consult special characters/help documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophes relative to other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is considered part of the word or number in which it appears; it should not be confused with a single closing quotation mark. When a word ends in an apostrophe, no period or comma should intervene between the word and the apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The last car in the lot was the Smiths’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the space and types of spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Spaces function as separators between words and sentences; there are regular spaces and fixed-width spaces (en, em, thin, hair) used in professional typesetting where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: En and em spaces match width of en and em dashes; fixed-width spaces are usually appropriate only in professionally typeset print and may not be supported in all electronic formats (see 6.120 and 11.2). For tabs and indents see 2.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonbreaking spaces and their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonbreaking space prevents certain elements that contain spaces from breaking over a line—useful for spaced ellipses, numerals that use spaces rather than commas as separators, preventing a numeral from separating from a unit (11.5 km), or preventing breaks between initials (E. B. White).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonbreaking space is Unicode no-break space U+00A0; widely supported in electronic formats. Fixed-width nonbreaking spaces are used in print contexts (see 6.121).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple punctuation marks combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple punctuation marks at the same location usually involve quotation marks, em dashes, parentheses, or brackets combined with periods, commas, colons, semicolons, question marks, or exclamation points; specific rules govern their combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules for quotation marks (6.9–11), em dashes (6.89, 6.94), parentheses/brackets (6.85, 6.97–101), and ellipses (13.50–58). See table 6.1 for common combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviation-ending periods with other punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abbreviation or other expression that ends with a period occurs at the end of a sentence, no additional period follows; when another punctuation mark is needed immediately after the period, both the period and the additional mark appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The study was. funded by Mulvehill & Co. Johnson et al., in How to Survive, describe such an ordeal. (Do not add a second period at sentence end.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods with question marks or exclamation points
rubrics_metrics.description: A period (aside from an abbreviating period) never accompanies a question mark or an exclamation point; the stronger mark takes precedence. This applies when the question mark or exclamation point is part of a title as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: She owned two copies of Will You Please Be Quiet, Please? (Do not add a period after the question mark.) See 6.125 for title-related issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with question marks or exclamation points in quotations and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: When a question mark or exclamation point appears at the end of a quotation where a comma would normally appear, omit the comma. However, when a title ends in a question or exclamation point, include a comma if grammar of the sentence normally calls for one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Are you a doctor?” asked Mahmoud. but in: “Are You a Doctor?,” the fifth story in Will You Please Be Quiet, Please?, ... (Comma after title may be retained for sentence grammar; may require rewording to avoid awkwardness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Question mark combined with exclamation point
rubrics_metrics.description: In the rare case of a question or exclamation ending with a title or quotation that ends in a question mark or exclamation point, include both marks only if they are different and the sentence punctuation seems essential; use this sparingly in formal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Have you seen Help!? Use such combinations rarely and avoid in formal prose (see also 6.72).

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles for lists and outlines (parallelism and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Items in a list should consist of parallel elements. Introductory numerals or letters may be omitted unless they indicate order, chronology, importance, or facilitate text references. Consistency is essential across similar lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This advice applies mainly to lists in running text; special lists (illustrations, tables, glossaries, indexes) have their own rules (see chapters 1, 14, 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Run-in versus vertical lists (when to use each)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, simple lists are usually better run in to the text, especially if the intro and items form a sentence; lists that need typographic prominence, are long, or have multiple levels should be set vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use run-in lists for concise items; set vertical lists for prominence or complexity (see 6.130–6.132).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting run-in lists (numerals/letters, punctuation, and separators)
rubrics_metrics.description: If numerals or letters mark divisions in a run-in list, enclose them in parentheses; if introductory material forms a complete sentence, precede the first parenthesis with a colon. Items are separated by commas unless any item contains internal commas, in which case separate items with semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When items are complete sentences or several sentences long, set the list vertically. Examples provided for mixed punctuation regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical lists: capitalization, punctuation, and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A vertical list is best introduced by a grammatically complete sentence followed by a colon. Two basic types: unordered (bullets or nothing) and ordered (numbers/letters). If unordered and items are not complete sentences, items usually carry no end punctuation and begin lowercase (except proper nouns). For prominence capitalization may be preferred; be consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If items run over multiple lines, assign a hanging indent to runover lines or insert extra space between items. For lists of illustrations/tables/glossaries/indexes see other chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered (ordered) lists punctuation and capitalization conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In numbered lists a period follows the numeral. It is customary to capitalize items in a numbered list even if items are not complete sentences. Closing punctuation is used only if items consist of complete sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Runover lines in numbered lists align with the first word after the numeral; use a tab to separate number and text (see 2.21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long, skinny lists (use multi-column layout)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid awkward long, narrow lists of short items, arrange short items in two or more columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for administratively enumerated measures or checklist-like items to make better typographic use of space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of runover lines in numbered lists
rubrics_metrics.description: In a numbered list, runover lines are aligned with the first word following the numeral; a tab usually separates the number from the text of the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps readability and consistent indentation across list items (see also 2.21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulleted lists formatting parallels numbered lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulleted lists are usually formatted in the same way as numbered lists with regard to indentation, runover lines, and capitalization/punctuation rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If none of the items in a bulleted list are complete sentences, items can usually begin lowercase (except proper nouns); choose consistent capitalization/punctuation approach across the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: When list format may not be best (use numbered paragraphs instead)
rubrics_metrics.description: When list items are very long sentences or include several sentences and the list does not require typographic prominence, format items like regular paragraphs each beginning with a number and a first-line paragraph indent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative to vertical list formatting when prose flow is preferable (see also 2.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical lists punctuated as a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: If vertical list items complete a sentence begun in the introductory text, separate items with semicolons or commas and put a period after the final item. Each item begins with a lowercase letter even in numbered lists; a conjunction (and/or) before the final item is optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons if items include internal punctuation. Such lists are often better run in to the main text unless highlighting is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical lists with multiple levels (outlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: For multilevel numbered lists (outlines) use numerals and letters for different levels; runover lines align with the first word following the numeral/letter and a tab separates the number/letter from the text. Each division/subdivision should normally contain at least two items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows up to seven levels with roman numerals, letters, arabic numerals, and parentheses; in shorter outlines one may dispense with some levels but ensure level distinction is visually clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended dictionaries for spelling and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: For general spelling matters Chicago recommends Merriam-Webster’s Third New International Dictionary (or its ongoing online revision) and Merriam-Webster’s Collegiate Dictionary; if more than one spelling is listed, Chicago normally opts for the first form listed to aid consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Collegiate disagrees with the Third International, prefer the Collegiate (newer lexical research). Use one source consistently throughout a single work; consult other standard dictionaries (American Heritage) as needed (bibliog. 3.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spellings peculiar to particular disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a variant spelling carries a special connotation within a discipline, respect the author’s preference (e.g., archeology vs archaeology); in absence of such preference Chicago prefers the first-listed form in the dictionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Webster’s separates equal variants by or; secondary variants are preceded by also. Respect disciplinary conventions when significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-US spelling in U.S.-produced works
rubrics_metrics.description: In English-language works by non-US authors that are edited and produced in the United States, Chicago generally changes spelling to American spelling (e.g., colour→color) to maintain consistency; in quoted material, however, spelling is left unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should usually make this change unless the author insists or a discipline-specific convention dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of chapter coverage (supplementing the dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: This chapter covers matters not easily found in dictionaries—forming plurals and possessives of certain nouns and compounds, how to break words at the end of printed lines, when to use capitals/italics/quotation marks for distinctive treatment of words and phrases, and when to use hyphens with compounds, prefixes, and suffixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See chapter sections (e.g., 7.89 for hyphenation guidance) and other chapters (12 for mathematics, 14–15 for bibliographic and documentation rules).
